name: Clinical strength antiperspirant
lead: Clinical strength antiperspirants are over-the-counter antiperspirants sold with higher concentrations of aluminium salts than ordinary products, aimed at people with heavy underarm sweating.[1] People use them to keep underarms dry, avoid visible sweat patches on shirts and keep odour down, which makes clothes sit and look cleaner through the day.[1][2]

Ordinary antiperspirants use aluminium salts to form temporary plugs in sweat ducts, and topical antiperspirants are listed as first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis in guidelines.[1][2] Treatment with stronger aluminium chloride products is described as taking about three to five days to show improvement, with skin irritation as the most common side effect.[2]
Members of T Nation have discussed clinical strength products from several brands in threads on underarm sweating.[3][4] Evidence specific to branded clinical strength products was not located.

paras: The term is a marketing category rather than a regulatory one. The higher strength is intended for excessive sweating of the underarms, and for hands and feet in some cases.[2] In the US, antiperspirants are regulated as drugs, while deodorants, which prevent or mask odour without blocking sweat, are regulated as cosmetics.[1] Wikipedia notes that apocrine glands in the armpits and groin, active from puberty, produce the sweat most responsible for odour once bacteria break it down.[1]

Aluminium salts such as aluminium chlorohydrate react with electrolytes in sweat to form a gel plug in the sweat duct, and also form a plug with keratin and have a mild astringent effect.[1] Wikipedia says antiperspirants are usually best applied before bed.[1] Hyperhidrosis treatment uses aluminium chloride products at much higher concentrations than regular antiperspirants, and improvement takes three to five days.[2]

The first commercial antiperspirant, Everdry, appeared in 1903, and Jules Montenier patented the modern antiperspirant formulation on 28 January 1941; it was sold as the spray Stopette.[1] Edna Murphey's Mum, patented in 1888, was the first modern commercial deodorant.[1] Gillette's Right Guard was the first aerosol antiperspirant in the early 1960s, and aerosols reached 82 percent of sales by the early 1970s before the FDA banned aluminium zirconium aerosol ingredients in 1977 over inhalation concerns.[1] By 1957 about half of men were estimated to use deodorant.[1]

Wikipedia reports that focal hyperhidrosis may affect up to 2.8 percent of the US population, men and women equally, most often at ages 25 to 64, and that more than 80 percent of patients report moderate to severe emotional effects.[2] Underarm sweat marks on shirts are the visible part of the problem, and people with heavy sweating may change shirts several times a day.[2]

Skin irritation is the most commonly reported side effect of stronger aluminium chloride products.[2] The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants.[1] Wikipedia notes that the FDA said in 2003 that data were insufficient to change the status of aluminium antiperspirants, that a 2014 review of 469 studies found little evidence that aluminium exposure raises Alzheimer's, genetic damage or cancer risk, and that the breast-cancer claim traces to a 1999 spam email; the National Cancer Institute says further research is needed on conflicting studies.[1] In 2020 the EU's scientific committee judged aluminium compounds safe up to 6.25 percent in non-spray products and 10.60 percent in sprays.[1] Aluminium zirconium products can react with sweat and leave yellow stains on clothing.[1]

Alternatives described include topical glycopyrronium tosylate (FDA approved 2018 for underarm sweating), oral anticholinergics, botulinum toxin injections that last about three to nine months, tap water iontophoresis, microwave therapy and surgery.[2]

No studies found specific to branded clinical strength antiperspirants. Wikipedia refers to evidence-based reviews of nonsurgical hyperhidrosis management and lists topical aluminium chloride as first-line therapy.[2]

lore.intro: On T Nation, clinical strength antiperspirants come up in threads by men looking for ways to stay dry.[3][4]

claims.claim: Clinical strength products cut underarm sweat
claims.believers: A 2008 poster said Gillette clinical strength cut way down on sweating in his underarms, though he said it worked 'kind of'.[4]
claims.experts: Guidelines list topical antiperspirants as first-line treatment for hyperhidrosis; no studies specific to branded clinical strength products were located.[1][2]

claims.claim: Blocking underarm sweat moves sweating to other body areas
claims.believers: A 2009 poster wrote that with clinical strength products his underarms were dry but sweating shifted to other parts of his body.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies were located on compensatory sweating from antiperspirant use.

claims.claim: Sweating on testosterone therapy shows up at the underarms and clinical strength products are used to cope.
claims.believers: A 2015 poster on testosterone cypionate, hCG and hydrochlorothiazide reported underarms soaked by 9 am at work and asked whether others had noticed more underarm sweating.[7]
claims.experts: No published studies were located linking antiperspirant products to testosterone-related sweating; hyperhidrosis guidelines list aluminium chloride products first.[2]

claims.claim: Certain Dri and similar over-the-counter brands are the clinical strength option to try.
claims.believers: T Nation threads on deodorants and underarm sweat repost a Certain Dri advertisement describing it as the top doctor-recommended clinical strength antiperspirant.[5][6]
claims.experts: The term 'clinical strength' is a marketing category rather than a regulatory one.[2]

card.summary: Stronger-aluminium antiperspirants for heavy sweaters; a step before Rx.
card.note: Irritation is the most common side effect.

quick.overview:
Clinical strength antiperspirants contain more aluminium salt than regular ones and target heavy sweating.

Sources found on branded products are thin.
quick.mechanism: Aluminium salts plug sweat ducts so less sweat reaches the skin.
quick.risks: Skin irritation is the most common effect. People with kidney dysfunction are advised by the FDA to consult a doctor first.

chain: Higher-strength aluminium salts plug sweat ducts
Less underarm sweat reaches the skin and clothing
Dry underarms and no visible sweat marks on shirts
angle.text: The product is applied to underarms to reduce sweat output so shirts stay dry and odour is lower. It is used by people whose ordinary antiperspirant does not keep up.

infobox: About three to five days of use[2]
